title: Medea
author: Euripides
openingText: NURSE. Would God no Argo e'er had winged the seas To Colchis through the blue Symplegades: No shaft of riven pine in Pelion's glen Shaped that first oar-blade in the hands of men Valiant, who won, to save King Pelias' vow, The fleece All-golden! Never then, I trow, Mine own princess, her spirit wounded sore With love of Jason, to the encastled shore Had sailed of old Iolcos: never wrought The daughters of King Pelias, knowing not, To spill their father's life: nor fled in fear, Hunted for that fierce sin, to Corinth here With Jason and her babes.
about:
Medea is the play in which Jason — the hero of the Argonauts, the man who got the Golden Fleece — abandons his wife Medea for a younger princess from Corinth. Medea, who left her own country and killed her own brother to help Jason, plans her revenge. Over the course of the play she destroys his new bride, kills the bride's father, and finally murders her own two children to make Jason childless. Then she escapes in a chariot drawn by dragons.

Euripides wrote it in 431 BCE. It is the most famous of his plays and one of the most disturbing of any Greek tragedy. Medea is given some of the most powerful speeches in Greek about the position of women, the nature of betrayal, and what an injured intelligence can become.

angleCards.title: Medea as argumentative genius.
angleCards.text: Before Medea acts, she persuades. She talks Creon into one extra day — the day she needs. She wins Aegeus's promise of sanctuary with a precision that leaves him no exit. She disarms Jason long enough to send the children in with their poisoned gifts. Every scene where she speaks to a man, she gets exactly what she needs. Read the play attending to how her arguments work — what she gives each man, what she withholds, how she reads the vanity or fear in each of them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Medea as a study in rhetoric and persuasion — tracking how she manipulates each man she faces and what this reveals about the men, not just about her.

angleCards.title: The mother's calculation.
angleCards.text: The decision to kill her own children is not made in a moment of madness — Euripides stages it as a deliberation, with Medea reasoning through it step by step, her maternal love fighting with her will to hurt Jason past any recovery. He gives her the argument and the counter-argument in the same speech. This is the most anatomised act of horror in ancient drama. Read asking: is she in control of herself, or isn't she — and does the play give you a clear answer?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to focus on the infanticide scene — how Euripides stages the decision, what Medea's reasoning actually is, and whether the play frames her as rational agent or overwhelmed victim of her own passion.

angleCards.title: What Jason fails to understand.
angleCards.text: Jason's defence of himself is not stupid — he believes it. He has made a good match; he will provide for his sons; he is building a future. He cannot understand why Medea will not accept this logic, because he has never understood what she sacrificed or what the exchange meant to her. The play's quiet anatomy of male self-deception runs through every scene Jason appears in. He speaks in the language of reason and gratitude; read what that language conceals.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play as a portrait of Jason — a man who genuinely believes his own account of events — and ask what Euripides is saying about the particular blindness of men who mistake advantage for virtue.

angleCards.title: A woman speaks for women.
angleCards.text: Medea's first major speech to the Chorus is one of the earliest pieces of feminist rhetoric in Western literature. She lists, systematically, the conditions of a woman's life in Greece: bought with a dowry, given to a stranger, required to adapt without guidance, unable to leave. She is not appealing for sympathy — she is making an argument. Read this speech as a political act, and consider what it means that Euripides, a man, put it in this woman's mouth.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Medea's opening speech as a rhetorical text — an argument about the structural position of women in Greek society — and ask how it functions within a play that also makes Medea a murderer.

cast.name: Medea
cast.description: A foreigner, a witch, and a woman who gave up everything for a man who has now discarded her. She is the cleverest person in the play — and the most dangerous, precisely because Jason has given her nothing left to lose.

cast.name: Jason
cast.description: The man who won the Golden Fleece and married Medea to do it, now making the sensible match with a Corinthian princess. He believes he is being reasonable. He is the last person in the play to understand what is coming.

cast.name: The Nurse
cast.description: The play opens with her — an old woman who loves Medea and is terrified of her in equal measure. She is the audience's first guide into the house, and her fear is more eloquent than any formal warning.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: The father of Jason's new bride, who banishes Medea from Corinth to protect his daughter. He knows Medea is dangerous and acts accordingly — but Medea is a better negotiator, and she gets her day.

cast.name: Aegeus
cast.description: He appears at the pivot of the play — a childless king passing through Corinth who promises Medea sanctuary in Athens in exchange for her help. He makes his promise in good faith, with no idea what he is enabling.

cast.name: The Chorus
cast.description: A group of Corinthian women who sympathise with Medea and promise to keep her secrets. They are the conscience of the play — they know what she is planning, they cannot stop her, and by the end they no longer try.

whyItMatters.title: A Woman Who Refuses to Be Pitied
whyItMatters.body: Medea's first long speech is about what life is like for women in marriage — the impossibility of choosing, the dependence on the husband's good behavior, the loneliness in a foreign city. The speech is one of the earliest sustained accounts of women's situation in Western literature and remains startling for how directly it speaks.

whyItMatters.title: Intelligence as Threat
whyItMatters.body: What makes Medea terrifying is not her violence but her clarity. She thinks through every step. She knows what she is doing. The play is honest that intelligence without an outlet for action becomes intelligence directed at destruction.

whyItMatters.title: A Tragedy That Does Not Punish
whyItMatters.body: Greek tragedies usually end with the violator destroyed. The Medea ends with Medea escaping in triumph, untouched. The play refuses the usual moral resolution. The ending is one of the strangest in Greek drama and one of the reasons the play has continued to be read.
